3	description: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and author the canon packs those facets earn. Use from a canon when a project's evidence shows a facet its shelf does not yet home — the curation stages' pack-writing method, and an owner's when asking what a project has taught the shelf.
4	---
5	
6	# Generate project instructions — extract packs, not a project doc
7	
8	Grow the canon's pack library using a project as the evidence, and decide here — never in the project —
9	whether an insight becomes a pack every repo can declare. Projects recur **along axes**, not as wholes:
10	the same working style with a different product, the same technology under a different working style. So
11	split what you find by axis — a facet later projects will share becomes a **canon** pack, and what stays
12	specific to *this* project lands in **its own local pack**.
13	
14	The deliverable is therefore **two kinds of pack**, never a single "how to work on this repo" document:
15	
16	- **Canon pack seeds and refinements** — one `packs/<facet>/` per facet where this project has real
17	  portable insight, each written as if this project didn't exist, proposed to Claudinite.
18	- **The project's own local pack(s)** — under `.claudinite/local/packs/<pack>/` in the project's tree:
19	  the project-specific working style, concrete values (real commands, paths, names, metrics), and the
20	  project-specific rules that *don't* generalize — carried the same way any pack carries them (a check
21	  in the pack's `rules`, an activity skill, prose in `RULES.md`, a scheduled task), not a thin doc.
22	  This is the project's normalized capture surface; its `CLAUDE.md` is a thin routing map to it, loaded
23	  through the pack system rather than `@import`.
24	
25	The failure mode this skill exists to prevent: investigating the repo and producing one competent "how
26	to work on this repo" document — real commands, real paths, this product's concepts — with the
27	reusable core never separated out and the project-specific core dumped as always-loaded prose. If
28	portable guidance ends up in a local pack (it should be a canon pack), or the project's file names end
29	up in a canon pack (they belong in the local pack), the split is wrong.
30	
31	## 1. Gather the evidence
32	
33	Read the project before writing a word: README and existing docs, `CLAUDE.md` and everything it
34	imports, dependency and build manifests, scripts and CI, the test layout, git history and recent
35	PRs/issues, and any conversation with the owner about how they want to work. You are collecting two
36	things, both grounded in what you actually find:
37	
38	- the **facets** this project exhibits (step 2), and
39	- every **candidate rule** — each convention, procedure, or quality bar the project works by — ready to
40	  be sorted by owner (step 3).
41	
42	Invent nothing. If a call that changes the outcome is genuinely open, ask the owner one focused
43	question (via the structured popup); otherwise take the sensible default and note it.
44	
45	## 2. Decompose into facets, and check the shelf per facet
46	
47	A project is a bundle of **facets**, each a candidate pack on its own axis:
48	
49	- **Class — the working style.** How work runs end to end: the loop by which a change is proposed,
50	  verified, and shipped; the production bar; audience and longevity. Test: the pack still fits a
51	  project on a different stack, for a different product idea.
52	- **Technology — the platform.** True for any project on that platform, whatever its class or product.
53	  Test: the pack still fits when the product and the working style change. The first project on a new
54	  platform mints its pack — an iPhone app arriving tomorrow mints `iphone-app` the same way
55	  `chrome-extension` and `aws-sam` were minted.
56	- **Aspect — a separable slice of concern**, usually with its own on-switch. `chrome-extension-release`
57	  is the same technology as `chrome-extension` at a different moment: the release/store standard a
58	  project declares only once it ships. Split an aspect out of its parent facet when its rules activate
59	  at a different time or under a different decision than the parent's.
60	- **Domain — the audience or setting**, when it changes how work is done. A children's-app pack would
61	  carry design-review, requirement-processing, and compliance rules that hold whether the app is
62	  Flutter or web; a regulated-industry pack likewise. A domain that doesn't change the working rules
63	  isn't a facet worth a pack.
64	
65	**The product itself is never a facet** — "this specific product" doesn't recur, by definition; its
66	rules land in the project's own local pack.
67	
68	And a *statement of what the product does* isn't a pack rule at all — not even a local one. A pack, canon
69	or local, homes **how we work**: the conventions, gotchas and review discipline that recur across tasks
70	whatever the feature happens to be. The working-discipline rules bar the requirement-shaped rule outright;
71	here, catch it wearing a convention's clothes — a rule asserting which entities exist, what a surface must
72	render, or that a feature's parts are wired to each other. Pack-worthiness
73	is a question about the *work*, not about how load-bearing the code is — a real gap in product coverage is a
74	requirements gap, and answering it with a pack is how a feature's spec ends up somewhere nothing executes it.
75	
76	<example>
77	One extension project can exhibit four facets at once: `spec-driven-product` (class),
78	`chrome-extension` + `node` (technologies), `chrome-extension-release` (aspect, once it ships) — and
79	its local pack holds only what none of them own.
80	</example>
81	
82	Then check the canon shelf **per facet** (`packs/` here; the mounted `.claudinite/packs/` in a
83	consuming repo — a facet already owned by a *canon* pack is declared, not re-authored locally):
84	
85	- **Covered** → declare it (technology facets are usually already declared from the fingerprint) and
86	  move on — unless this project's evidence **sharpens or contradicts** the pack, which becomes a
87	  refinement PR to that pack, not a fork. Each further project of a facet is another exemplar: the
88	  pack should read as the intersection-plus-union of all of them, and a rule only one exemplar
89	  supports should say so or wait.
90	- **Uncovered, with real portable insight in the evidence** → this skill mints it (steps 3–4).
91	- **Uncovered, but this project has nothing durable to say about it yet** → leave it; a pack of
92	  placeholders helps nobody.
93	
94	Write each facet down — a short name plus one defining sentence — before drafting anything; every
95	sorting decision in step 3 tests against them.
96	
97	## 3. Sort every candidate rule to the single facet that owns it
98	
99	For each rule from step 1, apply the **portability strip per facet**: delete from the rule everything
100	the facet doesn't keep, and see whether something meaningful survives.
101	
102	- Delete the product and the stack, keep the loop — survives? → the **class** pack (canon).
103	- Delete the product and the working style, keep the platform — survives? → the **technology** (or
104	  **aspect**) pack (canon).
105	- Delete the stack, keep the audience/setting — survives? → the **domain** pack (canon).
106	- Survives nothing → project-specific: the project's **own local pack**.
107	
108	Route each rule to **exactly one owner** — the facet whose whole population the rule serves. "True for
109	any Node service" belongs to the canon `node` pack, not to this project's class pack, even if every
110	project of the class happens to use Node. Rewrite what lands in a canon pack project-agnostically and
111	parameterized, the way research-project does ("read *input* as whatever it means for your project").
112	
113	Then gate **every** pack-bound rule — canon or local — on the promotion ladder
114	([engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md)): a rule a deterministic **check** could enforce, or a
115	procedure with a nameable trigger a **skill** could carry, becomes that (in a canon seed it's flagged
116	as a check/skill candidate; in a local pack you author the check outright in the pack's `rules`, with
117	a red-first fixture) rather than settling as prose. What remains in a `RULES.md` is the always-relevant
118	judgment core of its facet — write more checks and less prose. Dedupe against the corpus: a rule the
119	basics baseline, an existing canon pack, or a skill already owns is not pack material at all.
120	
121	## 4. Write each pack
122	
123	Mint a pack for a facet only when its surviving rules clear the bar — several durable rules, not one
124	stray (a single rule joins the nearest existing pack, or waits as a handoff note). Each
125	`packs/<facet>/` needs four things (mirror `research-project/` and `chrome-extension/`):
126	
127	- **`RULES.md`** — the playbook, addressed to the *next* project sharing the facet, on day one. Open
128	  with the facet's one-line definition and "a default to adapt, not a contract". Principle-first, each
129	  rule carrying its why. It loads at session start for every declaring project, so every line pays
130	  rent — cover the facet, not everything you noticed.
131	- **`pack.mjs`** — the manifest. Class/domain/aspect packs: `always: false`, `marker: null`,
132	  `detect: null` (declaration is authoritative). Technology packs: add the `marker`/`detect`
133	  fingerprint when the repo carries a reliable one, so `--init` seeds the pack into a fresh
134	  declaration; the marker only *suspects* a pack is wanted, it never forces its declaration.
135	  Discovery is structural — the directory is the registration.
136	- **`README.md`** — the pack's rule table (section ≤5 words | how enforced), plus one provenance line
137	  naming the project it was distilled from.
138	- **Index entries** — a row in [packs/README.md](../../../../packs/README.md) and, for a new pack kind, the
139	  matching line in the corpus map ([README.md](../../../../README.md) — there is no agent-facing corpus index). (1)
140	
141	The acid test before proposing any pack: **a reader must not be able to tell which project it was
142	extracted from.** Any surviving repo path, command line, or product noun marks a rule that belonged in
143	the overlay.
144	
145	## 5. What stays in the project
146	
147	The project-specific residue is not the canon's to take, and not the canon's to write: it lands in a
148	**local pack** under `.claudinite/local/packs/<pack>/` in the project's own tree, seeded by that
149	repo's adoption and filled by its own capture runs. What follows is the shape of that residue, because
150	the sort in step 3 cannot say "this stays local" without knowing what local looks like. Most projects
151	need **one** general pack (name it for the project); segregate a **second** only along the repo's own
152	**project structure** — a segment of the repo's tree whose work is its own territory (a `client` pack
153	for work under `client/`) — never around a technology or a methodology: those axes belong to the canon
154	(their portable half is a canon seed above; the project-specific residue lands in the structural pack
155	that owns the work). Each local pack is a real pack:
156	
157	- **`pack.mjs`** — `{ version, ruleRoutingGuidance, detect: null, marker: null, rules: [...] }`. The id
158	  is the directory name, the prose the `RULES.md` beside it and the skills its `skills/`
159	  subdirectories, all by convention — none of them is declared.
160	  A local pack is declared by hand, never fingerprinted or seeded (`detect`/`marker` stay null), as its
161	  namespaced token `local/<name>` in `.claudinite-settings.json`; its id
162	  must be unique and may not shadow a canon pack.
163	- **`RULES.md`** — the always-loaded judgment core and the project's concrete values (real
164	  setup/run/verify commands, real paths, inputs, metrics, invariants). Keep it terse; anything a check
165	  or skill can carry doesn't belong here, and anything inferable from the code is omitted.
166	- **Checks** (`rules`) — the project-specific deterministic rules as `.mjs` modules listed on
167	  `pack.mjs`, each with a red-first fixture (`test/pack.test.mjs`) runnable by the project's own test suite.
168	  Local check modules stay dependency-free (they must load without the gitignored mount): return plain
169	  finding objects rather than importing the engine's helpers.
170	- **Skills** (`skills/<name>/SKILL.md`) — the project's activity-scoped procedures, bundled in the pack;
171	  a local pack may also *require* a canon skill by name.
172	- **Scheduled tasks** (`tasks/<name>/task.json` + its `task.md`) — first-class like every other kind of
173	  pack content: the repo's own scheduler discovers a local pack's tasks in the same scan that finds a canon pack's,
174	  gated by the project's declaration exactly the same way. So project-specific scheduled work belongs
175	  in a local task declaration (a self-contained module honoring the task contract, with its
176	  co-located worker doc), not an out-of-repo routine and not a cron of its own.
177	
178	The project's `CLAUDE.md` becomes a thin **routing map** to its local packs (and its genuine design
179	docs) — it does **not** `@import` the pack prose; the pack system injects the active local packs'
180	`RULES.md` at session start, the same as the canon packs'.
181	
182	## 6. Deliver through the owner's approval gates
183	
184	- **Every canon pack seed or refinement → a PR against the canon.** Minting or changing a pack every
185	  repo can declare is the owner's call, and the PR is that gate — no corpus change lands unattended.
186	- **Write nothing in the project.** Its residue is its own to keep and its own runs to write; this
187	  method reads a project and delivers to the canon.
188	- **A project declares a new canon pack** only once it has merged and that repo's mount re-synced —
189	  declaring a canon id the mounted registry doesn't know is an unknown-pack settings error. Tell the
190	  project, don't do it for it.
191	- **Existing projects sharing a facet keep their local packs for now.** Once the canon pack lands,
192	  each one's dedup stage prunes what the canon newly owns; don't pre-trim against an unmerged pack.
193	
194	Close with a short report: each facet and its one-line definition, with its shelf verdict (declared /
195	refined / minted-to-canon / kept-local / left alone); the sort tally (rules sent to each canon pack /
196	the local pack / as a check vs. a skill vs. prose); and links to the PRs.
197

1	## What the mechanism lacks, by how many rows wait on it
     2	
     3	- **Nothing — the sweep.** 187 rows convert with the vocabulary as it stands. The
     4	  technology packs are where they sit (`macos`, `firebase`, `web-speech`, `headless-browser`,
     5	  `chrome-extension`, `research-project`): prose written before the declarative engine existed,
     6	  never swept. The bottleneck is the conversion sweep's throughput, not the engine.
     7	- **Skill triggers beyond file edits** — 61 rows. Tool-call triggers dominate (opening a PR,
     8	  filing an issue, committing, merging, dispatching a workflow, fetching from the web), then
     9	  owner-phrase triggers and tool-result triggers.
    10	- **Two-pass derive → assert** — 51 rows: a value captured in one place must appear, resolve
    11	  or be absent elsewhere; two files must agree; a declared pattern must select something.
    12	- **Action guards** — 38 rows: Bash command shapes (`git pull`, `git merge origin/main`,
    13	  `sleep`, `pkill -f`, `| tail`, `node --test` in the wrong form, `curl api.github.com`),

README.md
preconditions.mjs
task.json
task.md
=== task.md ===
     1	# Growth — promote lessons into the canon (the central stage)
     2	
     3	Read the target members' local packs, lift the portable lessons into the shared canon, and open a PR against the canon's default branch **for the owner to approve**. Declared only by the canon's home repo, so it runs **once, centrally**, never per project.
     4	
     5	The run's **Context section is binding scope**: it names the exact target members (those whose local packs changed in the window). Work exactly that list — the fleet enumeration already happened in the precondition; **do not enumerate the fleet yourself or widen past the Context**.
     6	
     7	## Conventions used in this doc
     8	
     9	- **GitHub access is MCP-only** (`mcp__github__*`). You are outside each member repo — read its files over the API (get-file-contents, never a cross-repo checkout: the shell's git can reach another repo, and not doing so is the session's granted scope rather than a missing capability). The canon PR is opened over MCP too.
    10	- **A member's local packs** are everything under `.claudinite/local/packs/` — its own packs, never the read-only mounted canon elsewhere under `.claudinite/`.
    11	- **`main`** stands for the canon's default branch.
    12	- **The canon shelf** is this repo's own `packs/` tree — the packs every member can declare. Together with any second corpus root the canon declares, it is the whole write surface below.
    13	
    14	## What each run does
    15	
    16	### 1. Read the target members' local **packs**
    17	
    18	For each member named in Context, read its **local packs**. The candidate pool is a local pack's captured knowledge — its `RULES.md` **prose** AND its own **checks** (a `<pack>/*.mjs` rule module — its id, description, and failure message *are* a captured, enforceable lesson; the strongest promotion lifts it to a **canon check**, generalized, reusing the [prose-to-checks](../../../claudinite-growth/skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md) mechanics — or to canon prose when it doesn't generalize to a check). **Out of scope, staying put:** a lesson deliberately placed as a **code comment at its call site**, a project's task scripts, product source, and config. Never promote from product source. A genuinely portable rule that looks trapped in a code comment was mis-placed at extract time — leave it for a future extract pass to re-home into a pack. You don't need to tell new from old — the dedup step drops anything the canon already carries. No barrier holds tonight's extracts: read whatever is already **merged** on each member's default branch; anything landing mid-run is tomorrow's input.
    19	
    20	### 2. Generalize each candidate — *before* judging whether it belongs
    21	
    22	Generalize first, then decide worthiness — never the reverse. The act of generalizing is itself the portability probe — a rule that goes vacuous when lifted, or only makes sense with its project's context, isn't portable; leave it local. Work the rule standalone (origin naming and grouping carry no weight); strip the project (names, files, example stay in the origin repo — promote the distilled rule only); a **technology** mention isn't a disqualifier (lift it to the broadest scope that stays true — tech-specific is fine, *product*-specific is not); decide tool-vs-process and frame it for that home.
    23	
    24	### 3. Then judge worthiness — deduped against the *entire* corpus
    25	
    26	Holding the generalized rule, decide if it earns a place by the bar [item-routing.md](../../item-routing.md) owns (don't restate its gates). Lean **inclusive** — keep anything a future project could use — but be strict about **duplication**: dedupe against **every** corpus doc, not only the one you'd expect to own it.
    27	
    28	### 4. Triage the mechanism, then route
    29	
    30	- **Descend the promotion ladder first** ([item-routing.md](../../item-routing.md)'s mechanism triage). Prose is the fallback, not the default: a lesson a check can carry is **authored as the check** in this PR — the rule module in the right pack, the failure message carrying the generalized lesson, **plus a fixture test proving it fires** on a violating input and stays quiet on a clean one. When a confident detection-plus-fixture can't be authored unattended, land the lesson as prose **and** open a tagged conformance-backlog issue — never a silently-shipped broken check.
    31	- **Route** each prose rule to its **one** owning doc ([item-routing.md](../../item-routing.md) owns the placement); match its voice and format; pick exactly one owner, never split or duplicate.
    32	- **A technology with no home → mint a fingerprinted stub pack, in its own PR**, reusing the pack-writing mechanics [the generate-project-instructions skill](../../skills/generate-project-instructions/SKILL.md) owns — `packs/<tech>/` with `pack.mjs` (add the `marker`/`detect` fingerprint when the technology carries a reliable one, else `detect: null`), a `RULES.md` seeded from the lesson, a `README.md`, and its `packs/README.md` index row. A minted pack is **not** shipped from this run — a run delivers on one branch, and a new pack earns its own review surface — so name the technology and the lesson that justified it on the tracker, where the pack-discovery pass picks it up. Never mint from imagination and never park an empty one to fill later — a pack minted here is populated from the *real, portable lesson* that justified it. Do not pad it with speculative rules no project earned — the "written from imagination, not distilled from worked examples" failure; an ungroundable rule isn't written. (Authoring a *fuller* pack from a technology's usage across the whole fleet — rather than a single lesson — is the per-repo pack-discovery task's job, not this floor's.) The follow-ups a fresh stub invites — enriching it from known best practices, triaging which skills it should require, spinning up dependent/aspect packs — are **not** automated here: note them for the owner and leave them to a later, deliberate pass.
    33	- **Write it terse — when + what.** State the relevance (*when* it applies) and the rule (*what* to do); add a *why* only to flag severity, in a few words.
    34	- **Bounded write surface — the canon's corpus roots only** (CI-enforced on the PR: the shelf, plus any second root this canon declares). Edit only the one owning doc — or, for a check-conversion, only the new rule module, its registration in the pack registry, and its fixture test. Don't "improve" unrelated rules while you're in there. The two bounded exceptions (both within the shelf): the new-doc path [item-routing.md](../../item-routing.md) owns, and minting a stub pack.
    35	- **Never bump a pack's `version` or write a `VERSIONS.md` row** — both are `pack-version-bump`'s to write once this change has landed, and it is the only writer of either. A bump here puts a code change into an otherwise prose-only diff, and strands whichever members took the first of two changes claiming one number.
    36	- **Deliver on the branch and pull request your item names** — push to `Target-branch:`, and onto `Target-pr:` where one is named (the round then joins the review already pending); open the PR against `main` on that branch where none is named — one PR for the whole run's accepted lessons. Never a direct push, never a search for an open pull request, never a branch of your own. Keep every commit and PR terse. **Put the issue reference in the commit message** (`Refs #<n>` for the tracker below).
    37	
    38	### 5. Log the run to the tracker
    39	
    40	Append a dated comment for every run that promoted at least one lesson, and for any notable rejection.
    41	
    42	## Tracking issue
    43	
    44	The standing self-improvement log is the issue titled exactly **`Claudinite tracker: Promote to Canon`**.
    45	
    46	- **Find it by that exact title, never a fuzzy match or a hard-coded number** (a bare number can dangle).
    47	- **Create it already closed if missing** — creation always lands an issue open and ignores a `state: closed` argument, so create it and close it in a second call. **Never open, close, or reopen it** afterward — its state carries no meaning; only the log does.
    48	- Log each run as a **dated comment** — not a sub-issue, so history accumulates in one scrollable feed — the date, and per lesson: the origin repo, the **ladder rung it landed on** (check id / skill / owning doc, with the named reason when prose was the fallback), and the generalized rule (or, for a notable rejection, the reason and the existing rule that already covers it).
    49	
    50	## What this task must never do
    51

=== logs-prune README ===
     1	# logs-prune
     2	
     3	## Why the declaration reads as it does
     4	
     5	Carried over from the declaration's comments when it became `task.json`.
     6	
     7	claudinite-growth task: logs-prune — retention on the `conversation-logs`
     8	branch. `agent_model: 'none'` with `code_work: 'node worker.mjs'`: the whole pass
     9	is deterministic code the scheduler runs as a subprocess — no agent, no dispatch
    10	issue, seconds of runtime. The same shape usage-fold already has over the same
    11	branch.
    12	
    13	WHY IT IS NOT PART OF growth-extract. Deleting a capture past retention is
    14	arithmetic on dates over an orphan branch — which is why the extract worker had
    15	to spend prose forbidding an agent to merge that branch or rewrite its history.
    16	Coupled to the opus run it also kept that run's precondition carrying a second
    17	arm whose only job was to fire the prune on a quiet repo, so a repo with nothing
    18	to extract still paid an opus dispatch on the nights one log aged out.
    19	
    20	WHAT MAKES AGE ENOUGH. The prune used to be coupled to a judgment step — an aged
    21	log got a final pass before deletion — so pruning on the calendar risked deleting
    22	a capture nothing had read. What removes the risk is the extract run's READING
    23	WINDOW, not a per-file handshake between the two tasks: growth-extract reads from
    24	the oldest end of the branch on every run, against a retention measured in days,
    25	so a capture reaches retention having been read. The extract-from-conversations
    26	skill owns that window; this task owns the arithmetic.
    27	
    28	The whole contract is this default export; the retention arithmetic it names is
    29	in preconditions.mjs beside it.
    30	A CLOCK crossing a boundary, not repo movement (the term beside this file):
    31	the prune must keep firing on exactly the repos that went quiet.
    32	It opens no PR: its whole write is remove commits on the non-default logs
    33	branch, which is outside the outcome taxonomy.
    34	One ls-remote, one fetch, one tree read, at most one push — against a branch
    35	whose size retention itself bounds. Seconds. The bound is protection against a
    36	hung network call, not headroom for work, so it sits just past the slowest
    37	plausible fetch rather than at the leash.

content.content:
=== web-users RULES.md ===
     1	# claude-code-web-users-support — working from Claude Code on the web
     2	
     3	- **A person asking to change one of their personal preferences** — edit their `<email>.md` in the
     4	  preferences store repo this pack names, never here and never in the canon; a project convention
     5	  in disguise belongs in the pack owning its subject, and a preference triggering a command owns
     6	  only the trigger phrase.
     7	
     8	- **A person asking to record their personal preferences with no file yet** — create it in that
     9	  store repo, named for their exact identity plus `.md`, case included: the reader opens
    10	  `<path>/<email>.md` and nothing else, so any other name is silently never read.
    11	
    12	- **A web session halt-gated on a missing toolchain requirement** — re-paste
    13	  [`environment-setup-command.sh`](environment-setup-command.sh) whole and unedited into the
    14	  environment's Setup script field, then rebuild; a project-specific step belongs in its own
    15	  pack's `env` declaration, never in that body.
=== store.mjs head 60 ===
     1	// The STORE this pack points at: where a repo's users keep their personal
     2	// interaction preferences, and how one person's file is addressed inside it.
     3	//
     4	// One resolver, because two readers need the same answer and must never disagree:
     5	// the session-start step that fetches a person's file, and the conformance rule that
     6	// says whether this pack is configured at all. Anything that grows a third reader
     7	// (a fleet sweep writing the pointer into a member) reads it from here too.
     8	//
     9	// THE SHAPE, on this pack's own entry in `.claudinite-settings.json`:
    10	//
    11	//   { "id": "claude-code-web-users-support", "config": { "repo": "owner/name", "path": "preferences" } }
    12	//
    13	// `repo` is required — the store is a repository, because personal preferences
    14	// belong to a group of people rather than to any one project, and a repo is the
    15	// smallest thing that can hold them for a whole fleet without living inside any
    16	// member of it. `path` is where they sit in that repo and defaults to `preferences`.
    17	// One file per person, named for their identity: `<path>/<email>.md`.
    18	//
    19	// Dependency-free and pure: the caller supplies the parsed config, so this module
    20	// touches neither disk nor network and is testable standalone.
    21	
    22	export const DEFAULT_PATH = 'preferences';
    23	
    24	// `{ repo, path }` when the config names a usable store, else null. Null covers both
    25	// "nothing declared" and "declared but unusable" deliberately: every caller's next
    26	// move is the same either way, and the difference is reported once, by the rule that
    27	// exists to report it.
    28	export function resolveStore(config) {
    29	  if (config === null || typeof config !== 'object' || Array.isArray(config)) return null;
    30	  if (typeof config.repo !== 'string' || !/^[^/\s]+\/[^/\s]+$/.test(config.repo)) return null;
    31	  if (config.path !== undefined && (typeof config.path !== 'string' || config.path.includes('..') || config.path.startsWith('/'))) return null;
    32	  const path = (config.path ?? DEFAULT_PATH).replace(/^\.\/+|\/+$/g, '');
    33	  return { repo: config.repo, path: path || DEFAULT_PATH };
    34	}
    35	
    36	// Where one person's file sits inside the store, as a repo-relative path. An address
    37	// only — whether it is read from a working tree or fetched over HTTPS is the caller's
    38	// business.
    39	export function fileFor(store, email) {
    40	  return `${store.path}/${email}.md`;
    41	}
    42	
    43	// Is this string usable as the name of a person's file? It becomes both a path
    44	// segment and a URL component, so an implausible one is refused rather than
    45	// traversed with: `../../x` as an "email" would address an arbitrary file.
    46	export const isUsableIdentity = (email) => typeof email === 'string'
    47	  && /^[^\s/\\]+@[^\s/\\]+$/.test(email)
    48	  && !email.includes('..');

content.content:
=== #319 397f45cf
2026-07-18 missingbulb
Fleet PR-opening workers: state the issue reference goes in the commit message (#327)

The promote / discover-packs / dedup workers told the agent to "reference the tracking issue" without saying it goes in the commit message, so the nightly promote PR (#319) put its ref in the PR body only and reded the basics task-lifecycle check. Make each PR-opening worker doc explicit: Refs #<tracker> in the commit, and why (CI gates the branch's commits on it). Docs only.

Closes #326
=== #309 679ee978
2026-07-17 missingbulb
Growth-promote: MV3 content-script/toolbar gotchas, non-PR CI read, AWS CLI access (#309)

Promote 4 portable lessons (origin: TLDR) into packs/chrome-extension, skills/git-github-advanced, packs/aws-sam. Refs #99.
=== #578 6b0669f0
2026-07-30 missingbulb
chrome-extension: convert the classic-content-script rule to a check (#578)

The chrome-extension pack's prose has always said a content script is
injected as a *classic* script — a top-level `import`/`export` in one
throws `Cannot use import statement outside a module`, in the HOST PAGE's
console rather than the extension's, so the script silently never runs and
nothing in the developer's own devtools says why. That is a static
signature in the artifact, so it converts (prose-to-checks sweep).

New blocking rule `content-script-module-syntax` in packs/chrome-extension:
- the judged file set comes from the MANIFEST — the paths a `content_scripts`
  entry's `js` array names, plus the same array on a
  `chrome.scripting.registerContentScripts(...)` call — never every source
  file, because module syntax is correct everywhere else in an extension;
- comments are stripped and string/template literal CONTENTS blanked before
  the judgement, so prose describing the trap and a code string a script
  builds can't fire it;
- dynamic `import(...)` — the documented remedy — and `import.meta` are
  excluded by construction;
- self-gates to [] when the repo carries no extension manifest.

Fixture test in packs-tests/chrome-extension/: three violating fixtures
(static import, static export, a registerContentScripts-declared file) all
go red when the rule is neutered, four FP guards stay quiet (the classic
dynamic-import loader, module syntax in a comment/string, the module service
worker and page scripts, a repo with no manifest).

Deletion test applied to the standing prose paragraph: it STAYS whole. The
finding's why/fix carry the rule, the host-page-console diagnostic and the
classic-loader remedy, but the paragraph also carries a second rule the
check does not enforce — listing the module's whole transitive import graph
under `web_accessible_resources` gated to the target origins, and having a
test walk that graph. A paragraph carrying more than the check is not
redundant, so it is not trimmed.

Refs #572

=== session-end.mjs ===
     1	// This pack's SessionEnd step — the second capture EVENT (skill-usage-metrics
     2	// DESIGN §3.3). The engine's SessionEnd runner (engine/hooks/session-end-command.mjs)
     3	// invokes every active pack's `session-end.mjs`; this one runs the same capture the
     4	// merge-to-main step runs, keyed to the issue the runner named (0 when it named
     5	// none) where the merge step keys to the pull request it landed.
     6	//
     7	// WHY it earns its place: capture at merge time sees only MERGING sessions, and only
     8	// up to the merge. This event captures the sessions that never merge — a review, an
     9	// investigation, a session that ended in a question — and the post-merge TAIL of the
    10	// ones that do. Both are conversation the growth lifecycle otherwise never sees.
    11	//
    12	// It can double-write with a merge capture, and that is safe by construction, not by
    13	// coordination: capture keys its delta on the SESSION ID across every prior file for
    14	// that session, so a second event for a session pushes only the entries after the
    15	// first, and a zero delta pushes nothing at all (capture-log.mjs, pinned by tests).
    16	//
    17	// Best effort. Nothing depends on this having run — every firing enriches the
    18	// record, every miss leaves exactly the merge-only behaviour. The runner swallows a
    19	// non-zero exit, so this reports honestly rather than pretending to succeed: a repo
    20	// with no `origin` remote, or no transcript on disk, simply exits non-zero and the
    21	// runner logs it.
    22	import { spawnSync } from 'node:child_process';
    23	import { dirname, join } from 'node:path';
    24	import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';
    25	
    26	const capture = join(dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)), 'capture-log.mjs');
    27	
    28	// The engine runner hands on what the harness told it about this session; capture's
    29	// own discovery (CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID, then the newest transcript) is the fallback
    30	// when the hook ran without input.
    31	const transcript = process.env.CLAUDINITE_TRANSCRIPT;
    32	const session = process.env.CLAUDINITE_SESSION_ID;
    33	
    34	// The issue this session was ABOUT, when its launcher knew one — the runner's
    35	// documented pass-through (engine/hooks/session-end-command.mjs). A hook firing
    36	// carries none and captures as issue 0; the scheduler's executor session runs the
    37	// runner explicitly at the end of its run and names its work item, so an
    38	// unattended run's log is filed under the task it ran instead of vanishing into the
    39	// issueless pile. Anything that is not a non-negative integer is ignored rather than
    40	// passed on — capture's argument validation is not the place to discover a typo.
    41	const raw = process.env.CLAUDINITE_SESSION_ISSUE ?? '';
    42	const issue = /^\d+$/.test(raw.trim()) ? raw.trim() : '0';
    43	
    44	const run = spawnSync(process.execPath, [
    45	  capture, '--issue', issue,
    46	  ...(transcript ? ['--transcript', transcript] : []),
    47	  ...(session ? ['--session', session] : []),
    48	], { cwd: process.env.CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR || process.cwd(), encoding: 'utf8' });
    49	
    50	process.stdout.write(run.stdout ?? '');
    51	process.stderr.write(run.stderr ?? '');
    52	process.exit(run.status ?? 1);

===== packs/claudinite-growth/tasks/rule-revalidation/task.md =====
     1	# Rule revalidation — re-probe this repo's local packs
     2	
     3	Re-run the probe behind every rule in this repo's **own local packs** that asserts a fact about the
     4	environment — the shape a harness call accepts, what the Action's token may reach, that an MCP tool
     5	exists, how a platform behaves — and correct what no longer holds.
     6	
     7	**The corpus is `.claudinite/local/packs/` and nothing else.** A canon pack this repo only mounts
     8	under `.claudinite/shared/` is revalidated in the repo that owns it: the next converge replaces that
     9	tree whole, so an edit there is lost either way.
    10	
    11	## The method lives in the skill
    12	
    13	How a claim is judged revalidatable, how it is probed, what the four verdicts mean, and how a
    14	`references.md` entry is reaffirmed are owned by the [**revalidating-rules**
    15	skill](../../skills/revalidating-rules/SKILL.md). Follow it; don't re-derive it here. This worker
    16	frames the unattended run around it.
    17	
    18	## What a run does
    19	
    20	1. **Enumerate** every revalidatable claim under the corpus above, by the skill's test. Most of a
    21	   pack is judgment prose and out of scope, so this set is far smaller than the corpus.
    22	2. **Probe each**, per the skill's two probe rules, and record what you ran and what came back.
    23	3. **Correct what is stale**, as far as each probe reaches and no further.
    24	4. **Deliver by the shared procedure — [deliver-pr.md](../../../claudinite-tasks/src/deliver/deliver-pr.md)**.
    25	   Title the commit and the PR `Claudinite growth: rule revalidation`; the commit references the
    26	   tracking issue so the `task-lifecycle` gate passes, and the repo's offline test suite is green
    27	   before you push.
    28	5. **Report every verdict in the PR body** — every claim probed, its verdict and the probe behind it.
    29	   This task rewrites the rules sessions obey, on evidence a reviewer cannot re-derive from the diff,
    30	   so the body carries that evidence in full whether or not anyone reads it. Never bump a pack's
    31	   version or write a `VERSIONS.md` row — both are derived on the base branch after the change lands.
    32	   There is no standing issue.
    33	
    34	A run that found everything still true opens no PR at all, and says so in its run log.
===== packs/claudinite-growth/tasks/prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md =====
     1	# Prose-to-checks — sweep this repo's pack prose
     2	
     3	Mine the **existing** prose of this repo's packs — each pack's `RULES.md` / `SKILL.md` — for
     4	always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Work the
     5	*backlog* only: prose this run's siblings already wrote is [growth-extract](../growth-extract/task.md)'s
     6	own upgrade pass, not this sweep's.
     7	
     8	**The corpus is `.claudinite/local/packs/` and nothing else** — this repo's own local packs. A canon
     9	pack it only mounts under `.claudinite/shared/` is swept in the repo that owns it: the next converge
    10	replaces that tree whole, so an edit there is lost either way.
    11	
    12	Convert prose to checks in a single PR.
    13	
    14	## The method lives in the skill
    15	
    16	The conversion method — how to spot an always-testable rule in prose, judge convertibility, author the check plus its **see-it-fail** fixture, and decide what stays prose — is owned by the [**prose-to-checks** skill](../../skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md). Follow it; don't re-derive it here. This worker only frames the unattended run around it.
    17	
    18	## What a run does
    19	
    20	1. **Pick convertible prose** under the corpus above — rules that govern **how we work** (not what the product does — see the skill's first gate), that are *always testable* (a deterministic condition a check could assert), and that no existing check already covers. Prefer the strongest, clearest candidates; converting one or two solid rules well beats churning many shakily.
    21	2. **Convert per the skill** — author the rule module in its owning pack, register it in that pack's `pack.mjs`, and add a **fixture test that fires on a violating input and stays quiet on a clean one** (see-it-fail is mandatory — a check that can't be made confident is left as prose, never shipped broken). Then apply the skill's **deletion test** to the prose the check now stands beside — a paragraph the check fully covers is deleted whole, never trimmed.
    22	3. **Deliver on the branch and pull request your item names** — push this round to `Target-branch:`, and onto `Target-pr:` where one is named: the round then joins the review already pending, so a reviewer who has not got to last week's work reads one PR, not three. Where none is named, open the pull request on that branch under the title `Claudinite growth: prose to checks`. Never search for an open pull request or pick a branch of your own. Either way the commit references the tracking issue so the `task-lifecycle` gate passes, and the repo's offline test suite is green before you push.
    23	4. **Say what converted in the PR body** — the prose converted and the check id it became, per conversion. That, and the commit, are the record; there is no standing issue. Never bump a pack's version or write a `VERSIONS.md` row — both are derived on the base branch after the change lands.
    24	
    25	## What this task must never do
    26	
    27	- **Never ship a check that can't be made confident** — the see-it-fail fixture is the gate; an unprovable rule stays prose.
    28	- **Never convert a rule an existing check already covers** — dedupe against the check set first.
    29	- **Never convert a statement of what the product does** — a rule asserting which entities exist, what a surface renders, or that a feature's parts are wired together is a **requirement**, and belongs in the project's executable spec and the suite that proves it. Such a rule is testable, so it passes the check-the-world test on its own; the skill's first gate is what stops it. Found in pack prose it is already mis-homed — leave it and log it, never cement it as a check.
    30	- **Never write outside `.claudinite/local/packs/`** — not the canon mounted under `.claudinite/shared/`, not a `packs/` shelf this repo may keep of its own, not the project's own code.
    31	- **Judging convertibility and authoring checks + fixtures is heavy judgment** — a check that reds on correct work costs every session in the repo, so convert only what you can prove.

1	# Growth — dedup local packs against the canon (per repo)
     2	
     3	Reconcile this repo's **local packs** against the shared **canon** it consumes (Claudinite, vendored read-only), pruning local items — a pack's prose line, or a whole local check —
     4	the canon now covers. It lands the run's prunes through a single PR against the repo's default branch.
     5	Often there's nothing to prune, and that's fine. The run's
     6	**Context** is **binding scope — not a hint**: do not re-decide or widen it.
     7	
     8	> This task only prunes local packs against the canon; lifting local items up into the canon is the central
     9	> promote task's job (canon-side).
    10	
    11	## Conventions used in this doc
    12	
    13	- **Default branch.** `main` stands for **this repository's default branch** — substitute whatever the repo uses.
    14	- **GitHub access is MCP-native.** Updating the tracking issue and opening the PR go through the session's
    15	  **GitHub MCP tools** (`mcp__github__*`). The unattended run carries no `gh` CLI and an empty
    16	  `GITHUB_TOKEN`, so never reach for `gh`/`curl`; and never clone another repo, which the shell's git can
    17	  still reach — that boundary is the session's granted scope, not a missing capability.
    18	- **The mounted canon.** The exact canon revision this repo currently consumes — compare against *that*, not a
    19	  live fetch. It is what `.claudinite/shared/` holds at the mount's stamp (a promotion is visible here only
    20	  once baselining has converged the mount to include it). Prune only against what the repo actually mounts.
    21	- **The dispatch's Context narrows the *yardstick*, never the local surface.** When the Context names
    22	  newly-changed canon packs ("Re-check local items against these newly-changed canon packs: …"), **those packs
    23	  are this run's entire yardstick**: every prune must cite a line or rule id from one of *them*, and you never
    24	  widen the comparison to the rest of the mounted canon. What is *not* narrowed is the local side — **every**
    25	  local item is in play against those packs, whatever it is about. (Local pack names are unrelated to canon
    26	  pack names, so there is nothing to match up.) A dispatch with **no** Context block carries no such bound: the
    27	  precondition emits the list only when the mounted canon moved, and its other arm — the repo's own local packs
    28	  changed — deliberately emits none, so that run compares the fresh local items against the whole mounted canon.
    29	- **The repo's local packs.** The set identified in [this pack's README](../../README.md#identifying-a-projects-capture-surface-its-local-packs) —
    30	  everything under `.claudinite/local/packs/`. That's the corpus this task prunes within; the
    31	  read-only mounted canon elsewhere under
    32	  `.claudinite/` is never a prune target, only the yardstick you prune *against*.
    33	
    34	## Start by reading the canon window diff
    35	
    36	**Code-work already ran** — [worker.mjs](worker.mjs), the deterministic first phase of this task — and wrote
    37	what the mounted canon **added** in this window into the tracking issue's body: per declared pack, the added
    38	prose lines file by file, and the ids of any checks the window introduced. Your dispatch names that issue.
    39	**Read it before opening a single local pack.**
    40	
    41	That brief is the run's *starting point*, not a second bound: the Context's pack list is still what a prune
    42	may cite, so a local item covered by an older line in one of those packs is a legitimate prune when you can
    43	quote that line. What the brief buys you is attention spent where the *new* coverage is, instead of re-reading
    44	a corpus whose lines mostly predate this run. It is complete except where it says otherwise — a file whose
    45	diff was too large to fetch, and a per-file line cap, are both stated in place with the remainder counted; go
    46	read those files directly.
    47	
    48	A window in which no declared canon pack moved says so, and that run compares the repo's fresh local items
    49	against the mounted canon as a whole — the same as a dispatch with no Context block.
    50	
    51	The [skill](../../skills/growth-dedup/SKILL.md) owns what to do with the additions: which are candidates,
    52	which prune nothing, and why a removed canon line is the reverse signal.
    53	
    54	## The method lives in the skill
    55	
    56	What to prune, strip, or rephrase; the keep-test (an item that says *more* than the canon stays; one that
    57	only says it in repo-specific names goes); how a canon **check** covers an item more strongly than prose;
    58	and the shrink-only discipline — all of that is owned by the
    59	[**growth-dedup** skill](../../skills/growth-dedup/SKILL.md). Follow it; don't re-derive it here. This
    60	worker only frames the unattended run around it.
=== dedup worker head 50 ===
     1	// The growth-dedup CODE-WORK: detect what the mounted canon changed in the window,
     2	// and write the brief the agentic phase starts from.
     3	//
     4	// A run woken by canon movement used to be told only WHICH declared packs moved.
     5	// A pack is a corpus, so that sent the run re-reading all of it for coverage that
     6	// mostly predates the window, while the thing that can NEWLY cover a local item —
     7	// what the canon ADDED in those days — was nowhere in the dispatch. Detecting it
     8	// is deterministic code over the commit records, which is code-work's half of the
     9	// task, not the agent's.
    10	//
    11	// Two kinds of addition, and the second is why a prose-only read is not enough: a
    12	// canon **check** enforces its rule on every session and CI pass, which covers a
    13	// local item more strongly than a stated line does, and it is invisible in the
    14	// prose corpus. The brief carries both.
    15	//
    16	// The channel is the REPOSITORY, per the code-work contract:
    17	// no code→agent data channel exists, so the brief is posted as a COMMENT on
    18	// the run's own work item, whose number code-work is handed as CLAUDINITE_ITEM.
    19	// The item is where the agentic phase is already reading, the brief describes THIS
    20	// window and nothing else, and both die together when the item converges — which
    21	// is the whole life the brief has. A standing issue would outlive it by a week and
    22	// then hold a stale window.
    23	
    24	import { writeFileSync } from 'node:fs';
    25	import { pathToFileURL } from 'node:url';
    26	import { makeGh } from '../../../claudinite-tasks/public/github.mjs';
    27	import { loadConfig } from '../../../../engine/checks/helpers/repo-context.mjs';
    28	
    29	const log = (s) => console.log(`growth-dedup code_work: ${s}`);
    30	
    31	// The window this task's own cadence covers — `due:weekly` in task.json.
    32	export const WINDOW_DAYS = 7;
    33	
    34	// A canon pack's file, in the two-root form: the mount prefix is optional because
    35	// the canon home runs this same code from its repo root, where the shared packs
    36	// ARE `packs/`. A local pack (`.claudinite/local/packs/…`) matches neither root
    37	// — deliberately: it is what this task prunes, never the yardstick it prunes
    38	// against.
    39	const CANON_PACK_FILE = /^(?:\.claudinite\/shared\/)?packs\/([^/]+)\/.+/;
    40	
    41	// A rule id as a pack's declared-checks.json spells it — `id`, the key that file
    42	// actually uses (`rule` is the settings vocabulary for overriding one, a
    43	// different file). A drift guard in the pack's tests parses the real
    44	// declared-checks.json through this, because keyed on the wrong word it silently
    45	// returns nothing on every real patch while fixtures stay green.
    46	const CHECK_ID = /"id"\s*:\s*"([^"]+)"/;
    47	
    48	// How many added lines one file contributes to the brief. A heavy canon week can
    49	// move a whole RULES.md rewrite; the remainder is COUNTED in its place, so a
    50	// truncated brief never reads as the complete set of what the canon added.

=== revalidating-rules SKILL ===
     1	---
     2	name: revalidating-rules
     3	description: Re-probe the pack rules whose truth lives outside the repository — harness tool contracts, token reach, whether an MCP tool exists, a platform's behaviour — and correct the ones that have gone stale. Use when a revalidation sweep runs over a corpus of packs, or when asked whether a rule's environmental claim still holds.
     4	---
     5	
     6	# Revalidating a rule against the world
     7	
     8	Most of what a pack asserts is settled by reading the tree, and a check goes red when it stops being
     9	true. A rule asserting a **fact about the environment** has neither property: nothing in the repo
    10	turns red when a platform moves under it, so the prose stays green and the cost lands on a session
    11	spent on a route that closed. Re-running the probe is the only thing that catches it.
    12	
    13	**This skill owns the method, never the corpus.** Which packs a run revalidates is its caller's to
    14	say — a task's `task.md`, or whoever asked. Take the corpus from there.
    15	
    16	## What counts as a revalidatable claim
    17	
    18	A sentence in a rule, a check's `failureMessage` or `fix` text, or a skill's procedure, that would be
    19	**falsified by a change nobody in this repo makes**. The three richest seams:
    20	
    21	- **The Claude environment** — tool contracts and their failure modes (what `Edit` requires before it
    22	  will apply, what a scheduling call rejects, what a search returns for a bare name), which harness
    23	  surfaces exist, what a session can and cannot see.
    24	- **GitHub permissions and API behaviour** — what the Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN` may push or label, what
    25	  a path refuses, which status a call returns, what a repository setting gates.
    26	- **MCP functions** — that a named tool exists, what its parameters are called, what it returns,
    27	  which server carries it.
    28	
    29	Also fair game: any rule naming a version floor, a runtime's behaviour, or an external service's
    30	response shape.
    31	
    32	**Not** in scope, and left alone without a probe: judgment and taste rules; rules about how a repo is
    33	organized, which a check already guards and a stale one fails loudly; product requirements; anything
    34	whose truth a reviewer could settle by reading the tree.
    35	
    36	## The probe
    37	
    38	A claim is revalidated by **executing the smallest thing that would distinguish true from false**, and
    39	reporting what actually happened — never by recalling what you know, and never by reasoning from the
    40	rule's own wording.
    41	
    42	Two rules bound it, and they bind every run whatever corpus it is working:
    43	
    44	1. **Read-only.** Probe by doing the harmless half: call the tool and read its schema, request the
    45	   resource, run the command that reports rather than acts. A claim whose probe would **write,
    46	   delete, merge, publish, notify, or spend a credential** is not probed — verify it against
    47	   authoritative documentation and say that documentation, not a run, is the evidence.
    48	2. **A probe you cannot run is `unprobed`, not disproven.** This session carries the reach its repo
    49	   was provisioned with, which is not the reach every rule was written under. A tool that is absent
    50	   *here*, a permission denied *to this session*, a network path the sandbox blocks — none of that is
    51	   evidence the claim is stale. Leave the rule exactly as it stands, log it as unprobed, and move on.
    52	   Rewriting a rule into "you cannot do X" because *this* session could not is the single worst
    53	   outcome available: it is unfalsifiable afterwards, and it removes a capability from every future
    54	   session.
    55	
    56	## The referenced rules — reaffirm against the recorded reason
    57	
    58	A pack's `references.md` (the [writing-pack-prose](../writing-pack-prose/SKILL.md) convention: a rule
    59	ending `(n)` cites entry *n*; a `- **(check:<id>)**` entry covers a check) widens what a revalidation
    60	can judge, because the entry records **what would retire the rule** — the one thing a probe of the

1	---
     2	name: writing-pack-prose
     3	description: How pack prose is written — RULES.md rules, SKILL.md bodies and check text in a Claudinite pack, local or canon — brevity, structure, triggerability, findability, and the per-pack references doc. Loaded for any edit of a pack's RULES.md or SKILL.md, and when landing a lesson as prose.
     4	metadata:
     5	  force-load-on-file-edits-paths:
     6	    - "**/packs/*/RULES.md"
     7	    - "**/packs/*/skills/*/SKILL.md"
     8	---
     9	
    10	# Writing pack prose
    11	
    12	Whether a candidate *qualifies* as a rule at all, and which mechanism carries it, is
    13	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)'s call — settle it there before writing.
    14	
    15	**Start from the foundation:** read the "Write each rule" section of
    16	[authoring-agent-docs](../../../basics/skills/authoring-agent-docs/SKILL.md) first — its
    17	principles (concrete enough to verify, motivation stated, what to do rather than what not to,
    18	the right altitude, emphasis reserved) bind pack prose too. This skill is the pack-specific
    19	layer on top of them, and doesn't restate them.
    20	
    21	## The ration
    22	
    23	Every rule in a `RULES.md` is paid for by every session in every repo that declares the pack,
    24	forever, whether or not it ever applies — so prose is rationed, and the ration is small.
    25	
    26	- **One sentence per rule, near 40 words**: the trigger, the directive, and a consequence
    27	  clause only where the rule cannot be applied without it. A candidate that needs a paragraph
    28	  to land has not been understood well enough to be a rule yet.
    29	- **An extraction pass adds at most two rules.** If more candidates clear the bar, write the
    30	  two strongest and drop the rest — they will recur if they were real.
    31	- **Split a rule that carries two situations.** Each situation is its own rule with its own
    32	  trigger.
    33	- A `SKILL.md` loads only when its activity is under way, so it may carry procedure at length —
    34	  but it is still rationed by the same test: every line must change what the reader does.
    35	  Method, steps and decision points belong there; anything a session must know *without*
    36	  loading it belongs in `RULES.md` or a check, and rationale belongs in the references doc
    37	  below.
    38	- **Moving a rule out of `RULES.md` into a skill** — only where the skill's
    39	  `force-load-on-file-edits-paths` covers *every* moment the rule is needed. A skill whose only
    40	  trigger is its description is picked by the model, not the harness, so a rule that must fire at
    41	  a moment no file edit predicts stays prose, however activity-shaped it reads. (2)
    42	
    43	## Shape a rule so it fires
    44	
    45	- **Keying a rule to its trigger** — open with the act the reader is performing, not the state
    46	  of the world the rule applies to. Nobody notices that "a value is unknown"; they notice they
    47	  are writing an encoder. A rule keyed to a state never fires, because nothing brings the
    48	  reader to it.
    49	- **Keying a rule the reader reaches while debugging** — name the symptom that sends them
    50	  looking ("A fetch to a host you listed failing in-browser"), not the act that caused it. By
    51	  the time the rule is wanted the act is over, and the symptom is what they can see.
    52	- **Keying a rule that corrects a misconception** — name what the reader wants ("Wanting
    53	  `import`/`export` in extension code"), not the wrong move they might make ("Reaching for a
    54	  bundler"). Someone who doesn't yet know the move is wrong won't recognise themselves in it.
    55	- **Phrasing that trigger** — use the words the reader would use for the situation, and put
    56	  them first and in bold, so the rule is findable by scanning the left margin alone.
    57	- **Choosing the unit** — one block per situation, not one bullet per rule. A reader arrives
    58	  holding a problem, so give them the whole decision in one place rather than a cross-reference
    59	  to three neighbouring bullets.
    60	- **Splitting a rule that only makes sense after the one above it** — don't. If the subject
    61	  needs a "that" pointing back ("Writing that record"), it is a clause of the rule above, not a
    62	  situation of its own. Split when a reader could arrive at the second rule without the first.
    63	- **Separating the blocks** — one blank line between rules. The block is what a reader lands on,
    64	  and an unbroken run of bullets makes them scan lines instead; the separation costs one token.
    65	- **Ordering a file of many rules** — past roughly fifteen, group them under headings naming the
    66	  surface each concerns, so a reader scans headings before subjects. A flat list that long makes
    67	  every bold subject do the work one heading would.
    68	- **Grouping that separates two rules which qualify each other** — add an explicit pointer from
    69	  the general rule to its exception, or the general one reads as unconditional. That pointer is
    70	  the one sentence a rewrite may add that its source didn't have; name it as an addition when

     2	### 6. Tell the members that evidenced the pack
     3	
     4	A pack is authored because a member's real files demonstrated the knowledge — so that member is the first repo that should be running it, and the sweep is the only thing that knows why. For **each** member the fleet view records at `core` or `supporting` prominence for the technology, open **one issue in that member repo**, titled exactly `Adopt canon pack: <name>`. Find it by that exact title first and leave an existing one alone — one issue per member per pack, converged, never a second copy on a later run.
     5	
     6	The body carries what the member cannot re-derive: **the evidence** (that repo's own files, the ones the pack was grounded in), **the canon PR** link, **the blocker** (nothing to do until that PR merges *and* this repo's next converge carries the pack — declaring a pack whose code is not on disk is a blocking `config` error), and **the action** once both hold: the `adopt-pack` skill, which declares it, asks its adoption questions and re-vendors.
     7	
     8	Two things it is not:
     9	
    10	- **Not the `add-packs` protocol.** Don't use that label or either of its converged titles — those issues are a member's `adopt-requested-packs` task's input, and pointing it at a pack no member's mount can carry yet is exactly the blocking error above. This is a plain issue for a human.
    11	- **Not a substitute for the fingerprint sweep.** `fleet-add-missing-packs` will suspect the pack in a member once it is in canon and its `detect` fingerprint matches. This issue is the immediate signal, carrying the evidence that sweep never had — and the only signal at all for a pack whose fingerprint is `detect: null`.
    12	
    13	A member the fleet view shows only at `vestigial` prominence gets no issue: it did not evidence the pack.
    14	
    15	If an issue cannot be created (no Issues write on that member), that is a **tracker line, not a failed run** — the PR is the deliverable and it already exists. Name the member and what failed, and open nothing here.
    16	
    17	The "member X should declare existing pack Y" note from step 3 stays a tracker note: the pack is already in canon, so the fingerprint sweep converges an actionable issue for it on its own.
    18	
    19	### 7. Log the run to the tracker
    20	
    21	The standing log is the issue titled exactly **`Claudinite tracker: Discover Canon Packs`**.
    22	
    23	- **Find it by that exact title, never a fuzzy match or a hard-coded number** (a bare number can dangle).
    24	- **Create it already closed if missing** — creation always lands an issue open and ignores a `state: closed` argument, so create it and close it in a second call. **Never open, close, or reopen it** afterward — its state carries no meaning; only the log does.
    25	- Log every run as a **dated comment**: the members swept; each pack authored (technology, the members that evidenced it, the rungs its rules landed on); the adopt issue opened in each of those members (or why it could not be); each "member X should declare existing pack Y" note; and, for a candidate you rejected, its name and why. "Nothing unhomed this run" is worth a line too.
    26	
    27	## What this task must never do
    28	
    29	- **Never widen past the Context member list**, and **never write to a member's tree** — the only thing this task writes in a member is the step 6 adopt issue, in a member that evidenced the pack it just authored.
    30	- **Never author a pack for a technology the canon already homes** — a stub counts as homed; note the "declare the existing pack" action instead.

     1	# Growth — discover canon packs (the fleet sweep)
     2	
     3	One weekly pass over **every member**: read what the fleet is actually built on, subtract what the shared canon already homes, and open a PR **for the owner to approve** authoring the pack that is missing. Declared only by the canon's home repo, so it runs **once, centrally**, never per project.
     4	
     5	**Your scope is every COVERED member** — one whose declaration parses and names at least one pack. Enumerate them once at the start of the run and work that list; a member with no declared packs is not running Claudinite in any usable sense and is not swept. Finding nothing unhomed is a perfectly good, common outcome.
     6	
     7	## Conventions used in this doc
     8	
     9	- **GitHub access is MCP-only** (`mcp__github__*`). You are outside each member repo — read its files over the API (get-file-contents, never a cross-repo checkout: the shell's git can reach another repo, and not doing so is the session's granted scope rather than a missing capability). The canon PR is opened over MCP too.
    10	- **`main`** stands for the canon's default branch.
    11	- **The canon shelf** is this repo's own `packs/` tree — the packs every member can declare.
    12	
    13	## What each run does
    14	
    15	### 1. Manifest each member's stack
    16	
    17	For each member named in Context, catalogue what it is built on and how it ships — grounded in that repo's files (dependency/build manifests, lockfiles, toolchain/config, CI and release workflows, packaging/signing scripts, source structure, docs), citing the concrete evidence. Keep one manifest **per member**, tagged with the repo it came from. Do **not** yet consult the canon shelf or decide anything about packs — this step only observes.
    18	
    19	**Never infer from "projects like this usually…"; if the member's own files don't show it, it is not in that member's manifest.** If something is present but appears vestigial or aspirational (declared but unused), include it and say so. Be **comprehensive over concise**: a later step filters and decides, so a true item you omit is lost, while an over-included one is cheaply dropped. When unsure whether something rises to an entry, include it with the `?` flag.
    20	
    21	Catalogue across **three axes**. Put each item under the single axis that fits best; when it genuinely spans two, place it under the primary and cross-note the other.
    22	
    23	- **Technologies** — languages and their versions, runtimes, frameworks, build systems, and the major libraries that shape how you write and build there (the load-bearing ones, not every transitive dependency).
    24	- **External services / APIs** the member integrates with.
    25	- **Deployment / distribution mechanisms** — how it ships and to where.
    26	
    27	For **each** item report: **name**; **axis**; **evidence** (the file(s), and what they show); **what it is in that member** (one line); **prominence** — one of `core` (the project is built on it), `supporting` (used but peripheral), `vestigial` (present but apparently unused); and a **`?` flag** if you are uncertain the item is real or correctly characterised. Prominence is a factual read of how central the item is *in that member* — **not** a judgment about whether it deserves any downstream treatment. Output each member's manifest as Markdown grouped under the three axis headings, one bullet per item with the fields labelled.
    28	
    29	### 2. Fold the members into one fleet view
    30	
    31	Merge the per-member manifests into a single list of technologies, keyed by the technology, each carrying **which members use it** and at what prominence. This fold is the whole reason the task is central: the same technology seen in four members is **one** entry, recognised on first sight, so there is no cross-run dedup state and no duplicate proposal.
    32	
    33	Drop anything no member uses at `core` or `supporting` prominence — a technology only some member's vestigial config mentions has taught the fleet nothing.
    34	
    35	### 3. Find the canon gap
    36	
    37	Hold the fleet view against the **canon shelf**. A candidate is a technology (or a domain the fleet shares) that:
    38	
    39	- **no canon pack homes** — and **a stub pack counts as homed**: if `packs/` already has any pack owning it, the gap is closed. The action for a member using a homed technology without declaring its pack is to note that ("member X should declare pack Y"), never to author a second pack; **and**
    40	- carries **real, portable working knowledge** the members actually demonstrate — a build/config gotcha, a toolchain rule, a procedure that recurs across them. Judge worthiness by the bar [item-routing.md](../../item-routing.md) owns; don't restate its gates.

    11	// runs on every PR: the corpus-roots-only boundary is true for PROMOTE alone — an
    12	// ordinary engine change legitimately edits anything. Nothing in the tree marks a

    12	`metadata` (the harness's own `paths` is a limiter on when it offers a skill, so it cannot carry
    13	this), the engine's PreToolUse guard holds a file tool aimed there until the session has
    14	loaded that skill, and this rule catches the edits the guard never saw (a `sed`, a heredoc) by

    16	`engine/pack_loader/path-scoped-skills.mjs`. A load is a `Skill` tool call or a `Read` of the
    17	skill's own SKILL.md. `skills-index-current` keeps the generated

    22

    24	|---|---|

    26	| [`adopt-pack`](skills/adopt-pack/SKILL.md) | adding a pack to a repo that already runs Claudinite: declare, interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land |

    28	The adoption skills bundle two more checks of the same kind, over the answers a member stores

=== writing-pack-prose references section ===
     1	  pack already carries, the one a check now enforces (keeping only the half the check can't see),
     2	  and the one whose mechanism has since been retired — a rule naming code that no longer exists
     3	  teaches a world the reader won't find.
     4	- **Rewriting an existing rule** — carry the source's own strength forward. A rewrite must not
     5	  weaken a rule, and it must not strengthen one either.
     6	
     7	## The references doc — where a rule's rationale lives
     8	
     9	A pack keeps **one** `references.md` beside its `RULES.md`, servicing all of the pack's prose
    10	files and its checks. It exists for maintenance and review — the periodic pass that asks
    11	whether a rule still earns its place needs the reason it was written — never for daily agentic
    12	work: no rule sends its reader there, and no session loads it. So it stays in the repo that
    13	owns the pack and never vendors: a member mounting a canon pack receives the rules, not the
    14	reasoning behind them, and the pass that reaffirms them runs where the pack lives.
    15	
    16	- **Adding a rule that has a rationale** — write the brief rule in `RULES.md` (or the skill),
    17	  and put the reason in `references.md`. End the rule with the bare marker — `… never a
    18	  filesystem walk. (3)` — and nothing else: don't name the references file, don't link it,
    19	  don't ask the reader to follow anything. Not every rule needs one; a rule whose reason is
    20	  self-evident from its consequence clause carries no marker.
    21	- **Writing the entry** — one bullet per entry, keyed by the citing file's own namespace:
    22	  `- **(RULES-3)** <reason>` for a rule in `RULES.md`, `- **(<skill-name>-3)** <reason>` for a
    23	  line in that skill's `SKILL.md`; the marker in the prose file stays the bare `(3)` and
    24	  resolves within its own file's namespace. Write the reason so a future review can **reaffirm
    25	  the rule from it**: what would have to be true for the rule to be retired.
    26	  - A **workaround** explains the issue with not using it, with the evidence (the failing run,
    27	    the error, the measured cost).
    28	  - A **technology guideline** cites the original documentation it derives from.
    29	  - An **owner decision** carries the language of the request that set it.
    30	- **Numbering** — numbers are stable identifiers, not positions: the next entry takes its
    31	  file's next unused number, a removed entry leaves a gap, and nothing ever renumbers (a
    32	  renumber breaks every marker at once). One entry may serve several rules in its file; a rule
    33	  may cite several entries (`(3, 7)`).
    34	- **A check's rationale** — the entry points at the check, since a declaration admits no
    35	  comment and no new key: `- **(check:growth-write-scope)** <reason>`, same reaffirmation
    36	  standard. There is no marker on the check side.
    37	- **Removing a rule or check** — remove its entry in the same change, unless another rule
    38	  still cites it.
    39	
    40	The `references-integrity` check holds the mechanism together: every marker must resolve to an
    41	entry in the pack's own `references.md`, and every `check:` entry must name a check the pack
    42	still carries. The `rule-revalidation` task is the mechanism's consumer — it reaffirms
    43	referenced rules and checks against their recorded reasons on its weekly pass.
    44	
    45	## Migrating an existing pack onto the references doc
    46	
    47	An existing pack — a repo's local pack, or a shared canon pack worked on canon-side (a member
    48	never edits the mounted canon) — migrates opportunistically, one pack per pass, whenever a pass
    49	is already editing it. An unmarked rule stays valid forever, so there is no fleet sweep to
    50	force and no straggler to chase; the check only judges markers that exist.
    51	
    52	1. **Create `references.md`** beside the pack's `RULES.md` on its first entry, not before.
    53	2. **Work each rule**: keep the act-time consequence clause inline; move review-only rationale —
    54	   the evidence story, inline issue ids, a cost the reader doesn't need mid-act — into an entry
    55	   and end the rule with its marker. Shrink-only on the rules side: a rule may lose review-only
    56	   rationale in this pass, never gain text.
    57	3. **Recover the missing reasons from history, source-first**: for a rule that states no reason,
    58	   read the commit that added it and that commit's PR and issue *before* re-reading the rule —
    59	   derive the entry from the source, then diff against what the rule implied. The commit
    60	   message, PR body and issue discussion are where this corpus already keeps a rule's evidence.
    61	4. **Never invent an entry.** A rule whose reason can't be recovered stays unmarked — an audit
    62	   or the `rule-revalidation` pass judges whether it still earns its place; a plausible-sounding
    63	   fabricated rationale would let a future review reaffirm a rule on false grounds.
    64	5. **Cover the checks** worth reaffirming with `check:` entries the same way, from their `why`
    65	   text and their adding commit's PR.
    66	
    67	## Evidence
    68	
    69	The commit and its PR remain the archive — dates, session ids, quoted exchanges and the story
    70	of the incident live there, never in the rule. What the references doc takes from them is only
    71	the **reaffirmable core**: the reason and the minimum evidence a future review needs to re-test
    72	it. Keep a measurement inline in the rule only where the number *is* the argument — a cost the
    73	reader wouldn't believe stated qualitatively.

name: writing-pack-prose
description: How pack prose is written — RULES.md rules, SKILL.md bodies and check text in a Claudinite pack, local or canon — brevity, structure, triggerability, findability, and the per-pack references doc. Loaded for any edit of a pack's RULES.md or SKILL.md, and when landing a lesson as prose.
metadata:
  force-load-on-file-edits-paths:
    - "**/packs/*/RULES.md"
    - "**/packs/*/skills/*/SKILL.md"
---

# Writing pack prose

Whether a candidate *qualifies* as a rule at all, and which mechanism carries it, is
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)'s call — settle it there before writing.

**Start from the foundation:** read the "Write each rule" section of
[authoring-agent-docs](../../../basics/skills/authoring-agent-docs/SKILL.md) first — its
principles (concrete enough to verify, motivation stated, what to do rather than what not to,
the right altitude, emphasis reserved) bind pack prose too. This skill is the pack-specific
layer on top of them, and doesn't restate them.

## The ration

Every rule in a `RULES.md` is paid for by every session in every repo that declares the pack,
forever, whether or not it ever applies — so prose is rationed, and the ration is small.

- **One sentence per rule, near 40 words**: the trigger, the directive, and a consequence
  clause only where the rule cannot be applied without it. A candidate that needs a paragraph
  to land has not been understood well enough to be a rule yet.
- **An extraction pass adds at most two rules.** If more candidates clear the bar, write the
  two strongest and drop the rest — they will recur if they were real.
- **Split a rule that carries two situations.** Each situation is its own rule with its own
  trigger.
- A `SKILL.md` loads only when its activity is under way, so it may carry procedure at length —
  but it is still rationed by the same test: every line must change what the reader does.
  Method, steps and decision points belong there; anything a session must know *without*
  loading it belongs in `RULES.md` or a check, and rationale belongs in the references doc
  below.
- **Moving a rule out of `RULES.md` into a skill** — only where the skill's
  `force-load-on-file-edits-paths` covers *every* moment the rule is needed. A skill whose only
  trigger is its description is picked by the model, not the harness, so a rule that must fire at
